newsitem.title: USA: Lott says no date in Senate on balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Lott says no date in Senate on balanced budget.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, Republican of Mississippi, said no decision has been made on the date the balanced budget amendment to the U.S. constitution will be brought before the Senate.

"We are looking forward to it coming before the Senate soon. We hope to be able to get an early conclusion. I have not set a date because I have to consult with the Democratic leader to see how much time they would need to make sure we have a full and fair debate," he said at a news conference.
Lott said he is in consultation with Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota.
Earlier Monday, Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch, Republican of Utah, said the measure could pass his committee and go to the Senate floor for debate next week.

Hatch predicted the measure would pass the Senate with the required 67 votes if all Democrats who pledged to vote for it during their campaigns did so. It was introduced with 55 Republican and 7 Democratic co-sponsors.
Last year, the measure failed by one vote in the Senate after passing the House.
In the House, debate could occur about the same time as in the Senate.
While it passed the House last year, Republicans acknowledge it faces an uphill battle this year due to their party's losses in the November election.
If the amendment clears Congress it must be ratified by 38 of the 50 states in order to become part of the U.S. Constitution. This process would take several years.

The White House is waging a campaign against the amendment with a letter to be sent from President Clinton detailing the problems a mandatory balanced budget would cause for the Social Security system.

The amendment would require the budget be balanced each year during peacetime and would make it more difficult to approve deficit spending or tax increases. Congress would need to muster a three-fifths vote to approve either deficit spending or an increase in the debt limit. Revenue increases could be passed only upon a majority of the whole number of each the House and Senate, a more stringent requirement than the current passage by a majority of those voting.
